opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things we think about every day. When you're building something like a new inference compute platform, the demand comes from all directions. You've got the hyperscalers, you've got the neoclouds and the sovereign AI initiatives, you've got enterprises who want to run models on-prem, and then you have folks talking about edge deployments. Everybody wants faster, cheaper, more efficient inference. So the temptation as a startup is to say yes to everybody.

But I think discipline is really important here. As a company of our size, you can't be everything to everyone. What we've tried to do is anchor on where we think we have a genuine, structural advantage, and for us that's the data center inference problem, specifically the memory bandwidth bottleneck. When you look at generative AI workloads, especially as models get bigger and people care more about latency and interactivity, the problem isn't raw compute. It's how quickly you can move data in and out of memory. That's why we went with a digital in-memory compute architecture, and that's where we focus our energy.

So the approach is to go deep with a smaller set of customers who really feel that pain: people running large-scale inference who care about tokens per second, cost per token, and energy per token. You partner very closely with them, you get the software stack right, you make sure the models they care about run well out of the box, and you prove the value in production. Once you've done that, the breadth takes care of itself, because the same platform can then extend to adjacent segments.

The other piece is building an ecosystem. We don't need to serve every customer directly. If we work with the right OEMs, system integrators, and cloud partners, they can take the technology to a much broader set of end users than we ever could on our own.

So to sum it up: focus first, earn the right to expand, and use partnerships to scale. The demand is a great problem to have, but how you sequence it determines whether you actually win.

r001.rationale: The response says a company of its size cannot serve everyone and should work deeply with a smaller set of customers first, identifying capacity as a constraint on breadth.

r002.rationale: It describes broad demand for faster inference and greater concern about latency and interactivity, and names tokens per second as a metric. It does not clearly connect widespread demand for real-time interaction to fast token generation across AI applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that we have to be really disciplined about it, because the demand is genuinely broader than a company our size can serve well all at once.

When we started d-Matrix, we made a bet that inference was going to be the dominant workload, and that it needed a fundamentally different architecture than training. That bet has played out. But the flip side is that now everyone running inference at scale wants to talk to us, and those customers look very different from each other. You've got hyperscalers, you've got enterprises deploying their own models, you've got the model builders themselves, and increasingly sovereign and regional players who want their own infrastructure.

What we've tried to do is anchor on the workloads where our architecture gives a step-function advantage, not an incremental one. For us that's generative inference, specifically the memory-bandwidth-bound part of the problem, the token generation phase where the compute is sitting around waiting on memory. Our digital in-memory compute approach attacks exactly that bottleneck. So the first filter is: is this customer's pain really that bottleneck? If it is, we lean in. If they're mostly compute-bound or latency-insensitive batch work, candidly a GPU may serve them fine, and we'd rather say that than stretch ourselves thin.

The second filter is the go-to-market motion. A startup can't build fifteen different sales and support organizations. So we've prioritized customers who are sophisticated enough to co-develop with us, who'll give us real production feedback, and whose deployments are large enough to matter. A handful of deep engagements teaches you far more than fifty shallow ones, and it builds the software maturity you need to go wide later.

And then the third piece is the software stack. Breadth ultimately gets delivered through software, not through hardware SKUs. If we can meet people where they already are, in the frameworks and serving layers they use, then one hardware platform can address a lot of demand without us custom-fitting every engagement.

So the short version: go narrow and deep now on the inference workloads where we're clearly differentiated, build the software layer that lets us scale horizontally, and resist the temptation to say yes to everyone. The companies that fail in semiconductors usually fail from trying to be everything to everybody too early.

r001.rationale: The response says demand is broader than a company of d-Matrix’s size can serve well all at once, identifying limited capacity as a constraint.

r002.rationale: It describes broad demand for inference and identifies token generation as a memory bottleneck, but does not say that widespread demand for real-time interaction makes fast token generation relevant across AI applications.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to be very focused. There’s a broad range of interest in AI inference, but as a company, we can’t try to serve every customer and every use case at once. We need to identify where our technology delivers the clearest value, work closely with those customers, and make sure we deliver a complete solution that they can deploy.

That means being thoughtful about the models they’re running, their latency and throughput requirements, and how we fit into their software environment. It also means being willing to say, “That’s an interesting opportunity, but it’s something we’ll address later.” You build a strong foundation with a focused set of customers, and then you expand from there.

r001.rationale: The response says d-Matrix cannot serve every customer and use case at once, presenting that limit as a reason to focus before expanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be very focused. When you build a technology that can serve a broad range of customers, there’s a temptation to pursue every opportunity. But each customer has a different workload, a different software environment, and different expectations around performance and cost. You can spread yourself thin very quickly.

For d-Matrix, the approach should be to identify the workloads where we can deliver the most compelling advantage, work closely with those customers, and make sure the complete solution works for them. Then we can expand from that foundation. It’s good to have broad demand, but we need to translate that demand into a sequence we can execute.

r001.rationale: The response says pursuing every opportunity can spread the company thin and recommends sequencing, but it does not identify limited capacity to support customers simultaneously as the constraint.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention real-time interaction, fast token generation, or their relevance across AI applications.
